practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an extrinsic factor that influences injury risk?
A) The athlete's age
B) The playing surface
C) The athlete's flexibility
D) Previous injuries
practice_questions.marks: B) The playing surface [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two elements of coaching/instructing/leading (1.1.2) that can reduce the risk of sports injuries.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: knowledge of techniques/rules/regulations / experience / communication / supervision / ethical standards and behaviour. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how weather conditions can influence the risk of injury for an outdoor athlete.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "cold weather increases injury risk"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "cold temperatures reduce muscle elasticity and blood flow, increasing the likelihood of muscle strains"). A further developed or second distinct explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add "wet conditions also reduce surface traction, increasing the probability of slips and falls leading to ankle sprains or fractures, particularly on grass pitches"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by "protective equipment" and give one example of how it reduces the severity of injury in a named sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): protective equipment is gear specifically designed to reduce the impact of collisions, falls or external forces on the body / to shield specific body parts from injury (2 marks for a clear developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a rugby player wearing a scrum cap reduces the severity of head contact injuries during scrums and collisions, meaning that a blow which might otherwise cause a laceration or concussion has reduced impact force (2 marks for a specific applied example with the mechanism of protection named; 1 mark for naming equipment without explaining how it reduces severity). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A grassroots football club trains on a waterlogged grass pitch in winter. The coach has limited experience and the players wear summer moulded boots.

Discuss how the extrinsic factors present in this scenario increase the risk of injury for the players.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two extrinsic factors with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: the waterlogged surface (1.1.3) reduces traction, increasing ankle sprain risk; summer moulded boots (1.1.4) are inappropriate for the wet conditions as they lack the deep stud profile needed for grip, amplifying the surface risk. The coach's limited experience (1.1.2) means they may not recognise these hazards or adapt the session appropriately. Both factors are linked together with reasoning.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but explanation limited or not applied to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A professional rugby club is reviewing its approach to injury prevention. They are considering stricter equipment checks, better referee training and improved pitch maintenance.

Evaluate the extent to which managing extrinsic factors is sufficient to prevent sports injuries in a contact sport such as rugby.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that extrinsic factor management (equipment checks, refereeing, surface quality, quality coaching) can substantially reduce risk, then counter-arguing that intrinsic factors (the athlete's age, flexibility, previous injuries, fitness level) cannot be controlled through extrinsic measures alone. A clear, substantiated judgement — e.g. that both extrinsic and intrinsic management are necessary, with neither sufficient on its own — is reached with supporting reasoning.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side with some application to rugby and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about extrinsic factors with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an intrinsic factor that influences injury risk?
A) The playing surface
B) The athlete's previous injuries
C) The quality of the coaching
D) The weather conditions
practice_questions.marks: B) The athlete's previous injuries [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two individual variables (1.2.1) that can influence the risk of injury for a sports performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from the specification list: gender / age / experience / weight / fitness levels / technique/ability / nutrition/hydration / medical conditions / sleep / previous/recurring injuries. Answers that merely restate the same idea score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer's level of arousal can increase the risk of injury during competition.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "high arousal can increase injury risk"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "excessive arousal causes muscular tension and impairs decision-making, meaning athletes are more likely to make reckless movements or mistimed tackles"). A further developed explanation or second distinct mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "very low arousal can also be dangerous — an under-aroused athlete may react too slowly to avoid a collision or fail to land safely from a jump"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by "direct aggression" in sport and give one example of how it can cause injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): direct aggression is physical force or violent behaviour directed at an opponent or person that falls outside the rules of the sport (2 marks for a clear developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that aggression involves physical force).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a basketball player deliberately pushing an opponent to the floor after a disputed call — the pushed player falls awkwardly and sustains a wrist fracture, an injury that would not have occurred within normal play (2 marks for a specific, applied example with the injury mechanism identified; 1 mark for a vague example without the injury mechanism). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old female sprinter has recently returned from a hamstring strain. She has been sleeping poorly due to pre-competition anxiety and has reduced her food intake to lose weight.

Discuss how the intrinsic factors present in this scenario increase the risk of re-injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two intrinsic factors with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: the previous hamstring strain is the strongest predictor of re-injury — scar tissue is less elastic than the original muscle and she is likely still compensating in her movement patterns; poor sleep impairs tissue repair, meaning the original injury site has not fully healed; reduced nutrition means insufficient protein for muscle repair and lower energy availability, leading to earlier fatigue and loss of muscle control. The interaction between variables is noted (sleep and nutrition both impairing the same recovery process).
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but explanation limited.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A male amateur rugby player has a high body mass index, a history of knee pain and poor match-day nutrition. He often arrives at training with low motivation and tends to play aggressively when his team is losing.

Evaluate the extent to which intrinsic factors are the main cause of injury risk for this performer, compared with extrinsic factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying multiple intrinsic factors (high body mass — increased joint load; previous knee pain — elevated re-injury risk; poor nutrition — fatigue and impaired healing; low motivation — reduced engagement with warm up and technique; direct aggression when losing — risk of foul play injury). Counter-argument identifies extrinsic factors (playing surface, quality of coaching, equipment, officiating standards) that independently or additionally create risk. Substantiated judgement — e.g. intrinsic factors are significant but interact with poor extrinsic provision, and neither category alone explains the full risk profile.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side, some applied to the scenario, an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: When asked to "compare and contrast" intrinsic factors, structure your answer around both similarities and differences. For example, both poor nutrition and lack of sleep impair tissue repair and increase fatigue — but sleep deprivation additionally impairs reaction time and coordination, which are risk factors unique to that variable. Examiners reward answers that use the precise specification vocabulary ("previous/recurring injuries", "nutrition/hydration", "technique/ability") rather than informal language. For aggression questions, always distinguish direct from channelled aggression — failing to do so typically loses a mark.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct order for the key components of a warm up?
A) Mobility, pulse raising, skill rehearsal, dynamic stretching
B) Pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, skill rehearsal
C) Dynamic stretching, pulse raising, mobility, skill rehearsal
D) Skill rehearsal, mobility, dynamic stretching, pulse raising
practice_questions.marks: B) Pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, skill rehearsal [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physiological benefits of completing a warm up before sport.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct physiological benefits from the specification: increase in muscle temperature / increase in heart rate / increase in flexibility of muscles and joints / increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons / increase in blood flow and oxygen to muscles / increase in the speed of muscle contraction. Answers must identify a specific benefit — "it prepares the body" alone does not score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why dynamic stretching is preferred over static stretching during a warm up.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "dynamic stretching is more active"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "dynamic stretching maintains the elevated muscle temperature achieved during pulse raising, whereas static stretching held in a fixed position can temporarily reduce muscle power output"). A further developed explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add "by moving through a full range of motion in a controlled way, dynamic stretching simultaneously improves flexibility and pliability of ligaments and tendons without the power-reducing effect of prolonged static holds"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of the skill rehearsal phase of a warm up and give one sport-specific example of an activity used in this phase.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the skill rehearsal phase involves practising the specific technical skills and movements of the sport at progressively increasing intensity, bridging general preparation and the demands of the main activity; it also activates neuromuscular pathways and provides psychological benefits such as increased confidence and focus (2 marks for a clear developed description with the neuromuscular or psychological element included; 1 mark for a basic statement about practising sport skills).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a sprinter performing acceleration runs at 70%, then 80%, then 95% of maximum effort, progressively loading the neuromuscular system and building confidence in their starting technique before the race (2 marks for a sport-specific, progressive example; 1 mark for a vague reference to "practising" without detail). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A school cricket team arrives at the ground 10 minutes before a match. Their coach insists they start play without a warm up.

Discuss the potential negative effects of not warming up on the physiological and psychological readiness of the players.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering physiological negatives (muscles remain cold and less elastic — increased muscle strain risk; ligaments and tendons are less pliable — increased sprain risk; blood flow and oxygen delivery to muscles is low — reduced contraction speed and power; rapid rise in heart rate places cardiovascular stress on the body) alongside psychological negatives (no skill rehearsal — reduced confidence and concentration; poorly calibrated arousal — anxiety or under-arousal likely; no opportunity for mental rehearsal of batting or bowling technique). Both dimensions covered with developed explanation and scenario application.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least one physiological and one psychological negative identified and briefly explained with some reference to cricket.
Developing (2 marks): One or two negatives identified but not developed or applied.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An athletics coach is designing a warm up routine for a group of 400m runners. She must choose between a full four-component warm up and a shorter version that skips the skill rehearsal phase to save time.

Evaluate the extent to which completing all four components of a warm up is necessary for injury prevention and performance in 400m running.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that all four components serve distinct purposes — pulse raising increases blood flow and muscle temperature; mobility reduces joint stiffness; dynamic stretching increases pliability and flexibility; skill rehearsal prepares neuromuscular pathways and provides psychological benefits. The counter-argument considers whether 400m running is technically complex enough to require a full skill rehearsal phase (compared to, say, gymnastics), and whether time constraints in a competitive environment justify abbreviating. A clear substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. that the first three components are non-negotiable for injury prevention but the skill rehearsal phase has relatively more value for complex-technique sports.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two components discussed with benefits applied to 400m running, and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points about warm up components largely descriptive rather than evaluative.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about warming up with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a component of a cool down listed in the R180 specification?
A) Dynamic stretching
B) Pulse raising
C) Skill rehearsal
D) Pulse lowering
practice_questions.marks: D) Pulse lowering [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physiological benefits of completing a cool down after sport or exercise.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct physiological benefits from the specification: gradually lowers heart rate / gradually lowers temperature / circulates blood and oxygen / helps prevent blood pooling / gradually reduces breathing rate / removes waste products such as lactic acid / reduces risk of DOMS. Vague answers such as "helps the body recover" do not score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how blood pooling occurs and why pulse lowering prevents it.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "blood pooling happens when you stop exercise suddenly"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "when strenuous exercise ceases abruptly, the heart continues pumping blood at high volume but the muscular pump in the leg muscles stops assisting venous return, causing blood to accumulate in the lower limbs"). A further developed explanation of prevention scores 3 marks (e.g. add "pulse lowering maintains gentle muscular activity — such as a slow jog transitioning to a walk — which keeps the muscular pump operating until heart rate approaches its resting level, preventing blood from pooling"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by PNF stretching and give one example of a sport where it is commonly used in a cool down.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) involves moving into a stretch, then isometrically contracting the target muscle against a partner or fixed surface for approximately 6 seconds, then relaxing and moving into a deeper stretch; the contraction fatigues the stretch reflex, allowing greater muscle lengthening than static stretching alone (2 marks for a clear description that includes both the contraction and relaxation mechanism; 1 mark for identifying PNF as partner-assisted stretching without the mechanism).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a gymnast uses PNF hamstring stretches in their cool down — a partner holds the leg in a hamstring stretch, the gymnast pushes against the partner's resistance for 6 seconds, then relaxes, allowing the partner to deepen the stretch and maintain the flexibility needed for splits and leaps (2 marks for a sport-specific example with the stretch rationale explained; 1 mark for naming a sport without the rationale). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A marathon runner collapses on the finish line and immediately stops moving. She does not complete a cool down.

Discuss the physiological consequences of stopping exercise suddenly without a cool down and how a cool down would have helped.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two physiological consequences of not cooling down applied to the scenario — blood pooling in the lower limbs causing dizziness/fainting because the muscular pump ceases; heart rate and blood pressure dropping too rapidly; lactic acid and other waste products remaining in the muscles, increasing DOMS risk and stiffness over the following days. The discussion also explains how a pulse-lowering phase and subsequent stretching would have gradually reduced heart rate and breathing rate, maintained circulation to clear waste products, and reduced DOMS risk. Both aspects of the question addressed with developed reasoning.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two consequences or benefits identified and briefly explained with some reference to the marathon scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points identified but not developed or applied to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A professional football club has introduced a mandatory 15-minute cool down for all players after every training session and match, including PNF stretching supervised by a physiotherapist.

Evaluate the extent to which a structured cool down routine can reduce injury risk and improve recovery in elite football players.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that a structured cool down provides significant physiological benefits (gradual heart rate and temperature reduction, prevention of blood pooling, removal of lactic acid and waste products, DOMS reduction) and that PNF with a physiotherapist is the most effective stretching method for maintaining and improving flexibility. Counter-argument considers limitations: DOMS risk is primarily determined by the type and volume of eccentric exercise in the session — cool down reduces but cannot eliminate it; the 15 minutes invested in cool down could alternatively be used for nutrition strategies (protein intake within 30 minutes post-exercise) that also significantly support recovery; and the evidence base for cool down in reducing injury rates specifically (as opposed to aiding recovery) is less conclusive than for warm up. A clear substantiated judgement reached.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side with some application to elite football and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely descriptive rather than evaluative.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about cool down with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a hard-tissue injury?
A) Contusion
B) Strain
C) Dislocation
D) Tendonitis
practice_questions.marks: C) Dislocation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between an acute injury and a chronic injury.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct differences: acute injuries are caused by a single sudden traumatic event / chronic injuries develop gradually over time through repetitive overuse; acute injuries have an immediate onset of pain / chronic injuries have a gradual onset; acute injuries are often linked to a single specific incident / chronic injuries are linked to repeated loading over weeks or months. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a strain and a sprain, giving one example of a sport in which each commonly occurs.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a strain involves a muscle and a sprain involves a ligament"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon, commonly occurring in sprinters who pull their hamstring during maximum acceleration; a sprain is a tear of a ligament, most commonly affecting the ankle ligaments in a football player who lands awkwardly on an uneven surface"). A further developed explanation that adds the tissue type classification (both are soft-tissue injuries) scores 3 marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the causes and symptoms of an ACL (Anterior Cruciate Ligament) injury and give one reason why it is considered a serious sports injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Causes (up to 2 marks): the ACL is typically injured through sudden direction changes (pivoting), landing from a jump with the knee in an uncontrolled position, or deceleration — common in football, netball and basketball; it is a soft-tissue injury involving a tear of the ligament connecting the femur to the tibia (2 marks for causes with mechanism; 1 mark for a basic statement about twisting the knee).
Seriousness (up to 2 marks): an ACL rupture typically requires surgical reconstruction and a 9 to 12 month rehabilitation period, meaning the athlete misses a significant portion of their career; it also increases the long-term risk of knee osteoarthritis (2 marks for a specific developed reason with evidence; 1 mark for a vague statement that it "takes a long time to heal"). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old basketball player has been experiencing a dull ache in the front of her knee for six weeks. It worsens during and after training sessions.

Discuss whether this is more likely to be an acute or a chronic injury and identify two possible injuries from the specification that could explain her symptoms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion correctly identifying that the gradual onset over six weeks, worsening with repetitive activity (basketball training), is characteristic of a chronic overuse injury rather than an acute traumatic injury. Two plausible named injuries discussed: patellar tendonitis (inflammation of the patellar tendon below the kneecap — common in jumping sports, nicknamed "jumper's knee") and a stress fracture (tiny crack in the patellar or tibial bone from repetitive loading — hard tissue). The distinction between soft-tissue (patellar tendonitis) and hard-tissue (stress fracture) injuries is noted. Both candidates discussed with their causes applied to the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correctly identifies chronic injury, names two candidates with brief explanation and some reference to basketball.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies chronic vs acute with limited reasoning, or identifies only one injury without discussion.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national rugby union governing body is developing a new player welfare policy following concerns about the long-term effects of concussion in the sport.

Evaluate the extent to which the risk of concussion and its long-term consequences should influence how rugby union is played and coached at all levels of the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation acknowledging that concussion is a serious acute soft-tissue (brain) injury with documented links to dementia and Alzheimer's disease (CTE in post-mortem studies of former players), and that this justifies strict return-to-play protocols, rule changes (e.g. reducing high-tackle height) and better coaching of safe contact technique. The counter-argument considers that rugby is an inherently physical contact sport — excessive restriction changes the fundamental nature of the game; that most recreational players will never develop CTE (the evidence base is drawn largely from high-volume professional players); and that effective coaching of safe technique and robust NGB enforcement of existing rules may manage risk adequately without rule changes that alter the sport's character. A clear substantiated judgement is reached.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side with some application to the governance scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about concussion with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
In SALTAPS, what does the letter 'A' (first A) stand for?
A) Assess
B) Ask
C) Active
D) Airway
practice_questions.marks: B) Ask [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two things a first aider should do during the 'Look' step of the SALTAPS assessment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: visually inspect the injured area / compare to the uninjured side / look for swelling / look for bruising / look for redness / look for deformity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why ice should not be applied directly to the skin when using PRICE therapy.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic point (1 mark): ice applied directly to skin can cause an ice burn / frostbite. Development (2 marks): the extreme cold damages the superficial skin tissues, causing a cold burn injury that could be more serious than the original soft-tissue injury. Further development with example (3 marks): add that ice must always be wrapped in a damp cloth or placed in an ice bag with a cloth barrier — for example, a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a damp tea towel applied for 15–20 minutes achieves the therapeutic cooling effect without skin damage. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the PRICE therapy protocol used to treat a sprained ankle immediately after injury. Give an example of how each step would be applied.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks (one per correctly described and exemplified step, maximum 4). Protection — e.g. prevent the performer from weight-bearing, use a support bandage or splint. Rest — e.g. remove the performer from play and stop all activity involving the ankle. Ice — e.g. apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes every two hours. Compression — e.g. apply a firm bandage around the ankle to limit swelling. Elevation — e.g. raise the ankle above hip height while the performer sits or lies down. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A rugby player is injured during a match. The physiotherapist runs onto the pitch and begins a SALTAPS assessment. The player is conscious and alert.

Discuss how the physiotherapist should carry out the SALTAPS assessment and what decisions they might make at each stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A thorough discussion covering at least four SALTAPS steps with explanation of what the physiotherapist does at each step and what the findings might indicate, including two contrasting outcomes (e.g. if active movement is pain-free the player may continue; if strength testing reveals weakness the player is removed). Some reference to decision-making based on findings.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least three steps correctly identified and explained with some decision-making discussed.
Developing (2 marks): Two or more steps identified but little explanation of process or decision-making.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point about injury assessment. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A football coach has two players injured during training: one has a suspected sprained wrist and the other is unconscious on the pitch after a collision.

Evaluate the extent to which having a clear understanding of both SALTAPS and DRABC allows a coach to manage sports injuries effectively and safely.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that explains how SALTAPS systematically assesses a conscious injured performer and supports sound return-to-play decisions, and how DRABC provides a life-saving sequence for unconscious or non-breathing performers. The response applies both protocols correctly to the scenario (sprained wrist → SALTAPS then PRICE; unconscious player → DRABC immediately, do not complete SALTAPS). A well-supported judgement is reached — e.g. that both protocols together provide comprehensive first-aid coverage, but that their effectiveness also depends on the coach’s training and calm execution under pressure.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both protocols described accurately with some applied evaluation and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): One protocol covered well, the other only briefly; limited evaluation or judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic first-aid points with no clear evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct description of hydrotherapy?
A) Applying alternating hot and cold packs to an injury
B) Exercising in water to reduce load on injured joints
C) Using electrical stimulation to reduce pain
D) Applying high-frequency sound waves to tissue
practice_questions.marks: B) Exercising in water to reduce load on injured joints [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two psychological effects that a long-term injury can have on a sports performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: anxiety / frustration / low mood / reduced confidence / fear of re-injury / loss of motivation / depression. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between cryotherapy and contrast therapy in sports rehabilitation.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic distinction (1 mark): cryotherapy uses cold; contrast therapy uses both cold and warm. Development (2 marks): cryotherapy applies cold alone (e.g. ice packs or ice baths) to reduce acute inflammation and pain; contrast therapy alternates between cold and warm water immersion. Further development (3 marks): add that cryotherapy is typically used in the acute phase immediately after injury, whereas contrast therapy is used later in rehabilitation to stimulate blood flow changes and accelerate tissue recovery. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the three components that must be included in an Emergency Action Plan (EAP) for a sports event. Give an example of each component.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks across the three components (allow partial credit). Emergency personnel (1 mark + example 1 mark): identifies who is responsible for the emergency response — e.g. naming the first aider and the person who calls 999. Emergency communication (1 mark): specifies how emergency services will be contacted — e.g. designated mobile phone on the touchline. Emergency equipment (1 mark): lists available equipment and its location — e.g. defibrillator located at the sports hall entrance, first aid kit in the referee's room. Full 4 marks requires at least three components identified with at least one well-developed example. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A swimmer returns from a shoulder injury and begins a rehabilitation programme. The physiotherapist uses a range of treatments over several weeks.

Discuss how different rehabilitation treatments might be used at different stages of the swimmer's recovery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion covering at least three different named treatments, linked to appropriate stages of recovery (e.g. ice/cryotherapy immediately after injury; ultrasound in the sub-acute phase to promote tissue healing; hydrotherapy to rebuild strength with low joint load; kinesiology taping for proprioceptive support on return to training). At least one psychological aspect (e.g. mental rehearsal to maintain confidence) also considered.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two named treatments with stage-of-recovery reasoning and some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Two treatments named but little explanation of timing or purpose.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant treatment identified. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A school sports coach is responsible for the safety of 30 students during a weekly athletics session. The school has no written Emergency Action Plan and no defibrillator on site.

Evaluate the extent to which having a well-designed risk assessment and Emergency Action Plan would improve participant safety at this school.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering the specific benefits of risk assessments (identifying hazards, applying control measures, considering group characteristics such as age and medical conditions) and EAPs (clear personnel roles, faster 999 response, defibrillator accessible) in the context of the scenario, then challenging with counter-arguments (e.g. having documents does not guarantee they are followed; staff still need training; documents alone do not prevent all injuries). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. that both tools are necessary but insufficient without staff training and regular review.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both tools discussed with some scenario application and a partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly descriptive with limited evaluation or judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic safety points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a symptom of asthma?
A) Increased thirst
B) Wheezing
C) Slow-healing cuts
D) Extreme tiredness
practice_questions.marks: B) Wheezing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Type 1 — body cannot produce insulin; Type 2 — body does not produce enough insulin or insulin does not work properly. Type 1 — typically diagnosed in childhood/young adulthood; Type 2 — more commonly diagnosed in adults. Type 1 — autoimmune cause; Type 2 — strongly linked to lifestyle factors such as poor diet and physical inactivity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what hypoglycaemia is and how it should be treated during a sports session.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Definition (1 mark): hypoglycaemia is when blood sugar falls below the normal range / is dangerously low. Symptoms (1 mark): symptoms include shakiness, sweating, dizziness or confusion. Treatment (1 mark): treat immediately with fast-acting glucose — e.g. glucose tablets or a sugary drink — and stop the activity until blood sugar returns to a safe level. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a coach should manage a performer who has an asthma attack during a training session. Give an example of what the coach should do if the inhaler does not work.
practice_questions.marks: Management (up to 3 marks): stop the activity and ensure the performer sits upright (1 mark); provide reassurance to reduce anxiety (1 mark); help the performer use their reliever inhaler — up to 10 puffs, one puff every 30 to 60 seconds (1 mark). Example of inhaler failure (1 mark): if symptoms do not improve after 10 puffs of the inhaler, or if the performer becomes very distressed or their lips turn blue, call 999 immediately. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A gymnastics coach has two performers in her squad: one has asthma and one has Type 1 diabetes. Both conditions can affect performance and safety during training.

Discuss the measures the coach should take to manage both conditions safely during a gymnastics training session.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion of measures for both conditions. Asthma: confirm inhaler is accessible, ensure thorough warm-up, recognise symptoms and treatment protocol. Diabetes: pre-session blood glucose check, fast-acting carbohydrates available, signs of a hypo, communication with performer about their management plan. At least one contrasting point — e.g. the coach can take all the right steps, but the performer themselves must also take responsibility for managing their condition. Some comparison or discussion of both conditions' impact on session design.
Secure (3–4 marks): Measures for both conditions identified and some explanation, with limited comparison.
Developing (2 marks): Measures for one condition only, or both mentioned but without detail.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point about either condition. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A secondary school PE department is considering whether students with asthma or diabetes should be allowed to participate in all physical activities without restriction.

Evaluate the extent to which students with asthma or diabetes should be included in all physical activities, and what measures are needed to make this safe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing for inclusion (physical activity has proven benefits for both conditions — exercise improves lung function over time in asthma; regular activity improves insulin sensitivity and blood glucose control in Type 2 diabetes) contrasted with realistic risks (exercise triggers asthma attacks; exercise lowers blood sugar and can cause dangerous hypos in Type 1 diabetics). Specific measures are then evaluated (inhaler on site, blood sugar checks, warm-up protocols, emergency plans) and a judgement reached — e.g. that full inclusion is the right approach when appropriate management protocols are in place, but blanket inclusion without individual risk assessment is not responsible.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments for and against explored, measures described, partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists measures with limited evaluation or judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a symptom of sudden cardiac arrest?
A) Crushing chest pain with the performer still conscious
B) Staring blankly and fluttering eyelids
C) Unconsciousness and breathing difficulties
D) Wheezing and tightness in the chest
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconsciousness and breathing difficulties [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two triggers for an epileptic seizure that are relevant in a sporting context.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: severe head injuries / anxiety or stress / tiredness or lack of sleep. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a heart attack and sudden cardiac arrest.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic distinction (1 mark): in a heart attack the heart keeps beating; in cardiac arrest it stops. Development of heart attack (1 mark): a heart attack is caused by a blockage in a coronary artery that stops blood reaching part of the heart muscle — the performer is typically conscious and may feel crushing chest pain. Development of cardiac arrest (1 mark): sudden cardiac arrest is an electrical failure of the heart — the heart stops pumping effectively, the performer is unconscious and not breathing normally. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a first aider should treat a young athlete who collapses during a race and is suspected to be in sudden cardiac arrest. Give an example of how the AED would be used.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Call 999 immediately (1 mark). Begin CPR — 30 chest compressions (5–6 cm deep, centre of chest) to 2 rescue breaths, at 100–120 compressions per minute (1 mark). Retrieve the AED as soon as possible and switch it on (1 mark). AED example (1 mark): the AED gives voice instructions — attach the pads to the bare chest as shown, stand clear while it analyses the heart rhythm, and deliver the shock if prompted; resume CPR immediately after the shock and continue until paramedics arrive. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A swimming club coach is concerned about the risk of medical emergencies during competitive galas attended by up to 200 spectators and 80 swimmers.

Discuss the measures the club should take to manage the risk of epileptic seizures and sudden cardiac arrest during competitive events.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion of measures for both conditions. For epilepsy: pre-event disclosure of seizure plans, adapted supervision near water, designated first aider who knows the protocol, what to do during a seizure (do not restrain, protect from injury, recovery position, 999 if over 5 minutes). For SCA: AED on site and accessible, staff CPR-trained, Emergency Action Plan with named personnel and communication plan, screening of performers. At least one contrast — e.g. having equipment and plans is essential but only effective if staff are trained and confident to use them.
Secure (3–4 marks): Measures for both conditions described with some explanation.
Developing (2 marks): One condition covered adequately, the other only briefly.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant safety measure. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Every year, young athletes suffer sudden cardiac arrest during sport. Many do not survive because bystanders do not act quickly enough or the right equipment is not available.

Evaluate the extent to which having trained staff and defibrillators at all sporting venues would reduce deaths from sudden cardiac arrest in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that trained staff and on-site AEDs significantly improve survival rates (evidence: survival rates can exceed 70% when CPR and defibrillation are started within 3–5 minutes, compared to less than 10% when emergency services arrive first). Counter-arguments should include: cost and maintenance of AEDs, need for regular retraining, the fact that most cardiac arrests still occur without warning despite screening, and that lifestyle changes and pre-participation screening may be more preventive. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the relative importance of different strategies.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides explored with some application; partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists benefits without counter-argument or clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
At what core body temperature does hypothermia begin?
A) Below 37°C
B) Below 36°C
C) Below 35°C
D) Below 34°C
practice_questions.marks: C) Below 35°C [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two symptoms of heat exhaustion.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: excessive sweating / headache or dizziness / being very thirsty / feeling or being sick / rapid pulse and/or rapid breathing. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a performer suffering from hypothermia should not be warmed using a hot bath or hot water bottle.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic point (1 mark): a hot bath or hot water bottle must not be used to treat hypothermia. Reason (2 marks): rapid heat causes blood vessels near the skin surface to dilate (vasodilate) suddenly. Further development (3 marks): this causes cold blood from the periphery — the arms, legs and skin surface — to rush back to the core all at once, which can cause dangerous cardiac complications and a sudden further drop in core temperature. Warming must therefore be gradual and gentle. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the causes and treatment of dehydration in sport. Give an example of when rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone.
practice_questions.marks: Cause (1 mark): dehydration is caused by loss of bodily fluids — primarily through sweating during exercise — that are not replaced. Treatment (2 marks): drink plenty of water as the first-line treatment (1 mark); use rehydration sachets to restore fluid and electrolyte balance in cases of significant fluid loss (1 mark). Example (1 mark): rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone after a marathon or long-distance endurance event where significant sweating has caused both fluid and electrolyte depletion — replacing water alone without electrolytes can dilute blood sodium and cause hyponatraemia. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A junior football team trains on an exposed pitch on a cold, wet January afternoon. The coach notices that two players are showing signs of hypothermia, and later in the session a third player complains of feeling thirsty and dizzy.

Discuss how the coach should respond to these three players and what measures should be in place to prevent these conditions occurring at future sessions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion covering correct treatment for both hypothermia (remove wet clothing, wrap in blankets covering head, warm non-alcoholic sugary drink, avoid hot bath / hot water bottle / rubbing) and dehydration/possible heat exhaustion (drink water, rest, move to shelter). Prevention discussed with at least two specific measures for future sessions — e.g. mandatory warm kit policy, weather checks before training, drink breaks built into the session plan, risk assessment for cold-weather training. At least one contrast — e.g. the session plan alone cannot prevent all environmental conditions, but an Emergency Action Plan ensures the response is immediate when incidents occur.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both conditions addressed with treatment and some prevention.
Developing (2 marks): One condition treated adequately, prevention vague.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Three environmental medical conditions — hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration — are all linked to external factors that coaches can influence through planning and preparation.

Evaluate the extent to which effective planning and risk assessment by a coach can prevent these three conditions from occurring during outdoor sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A well-structured evaluation arguing that planning reduces risk significantly — risk assessments identify weather hazards, appropriate clothing policies prevent hypothermia, mandatory hydration breaks and water provision prevent dehydration, session scheduling in cooler periods reduces heat exhaustion risk, and Emergency Action Plans ensure rapid response when conditions deteriorate. Counter-arguments then challenge the extent of control: weather is unpredictable, performers arrive with pre-existing dehydration or inadequate kit, coaches cannot control individual hydration habits, and some environmental conditions deteriorate suddenly during a session. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about what planning can realistically achieve versus what remains outside the coach's control.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments on both sides with some application to the scenario and a partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists preventive measures without counter-argument or clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
